_**User**_

Many times in a notebook there's difficulty determining which order cells must be executed in, and in particular if you only want to run a particular cell which cells it depends on. Currently I use the right-click on each variable -> "Go to Definition" for variables that are missing (which I see from the error after trying to run the target cell). This is tedious and manual, as the cell that "Go to Definition" jumps to may also depend on other cells, etc. Add a feature to this extension that allows right-clicking on a notebook code cell clicking "Dependency Chain: Show Dependant Cells": this should highlight cells that this cell immediately depends on (1-jump cells) and highlight them in bright orange with a bright orange "1", then compute the (2-jump cells) and highlight them in fainter orange highlight and a "2", continuing on until the minimum set of cells to be ran are highlighted. This computed dependency tree should also appear in a new custom "Dependency Chain" view and clicking elements in the tree should jump to those cells in the notebook. In the "Dependency Chain" view a history of the past 10 dependency chains should be selectable without recomputation so the user can look back at recent changes. When a chain is selected in the view it should switch the highlighting and numbering in the notebook to only those for the selected chain.

---

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The first step is understanding how notebook cell decorations and tree views are structured in this extension.

Text editor decorations only work while the cell editor is visible. For multi-cell highlighting, notebook cell decorations or status bar items are needed instead. The next step is examining existing patterns like git diff highlighting, cell status bars, and tree view jumpbacks. The VS Code notebook API for creating cell status bar items is also being reviewed.

Checking the VS Code API for notebook cell decorations and the extension's target version. Dependency analysis will follow standard Jupyter tools like nbdime.

Static dependency analysis will parse each cell with Python AST to identify defined and used names. For a target cell, the latest preceding cell defining each required variable will be identified. This follows notebook execution order where the last definition wins, matching the existing "Go to Definition" jump behavior.

Pylance treats notebook cells as a concatenated module, jumping to the most recent assignment of a symbol above the current cell. The user's workflow reveals a transitive dependency problem: resolving one missing variable may reveal another missing variable in the cell that was jumped to. The feature must therefore compute the full transitive closure of all cells that define symbols used by the target cell, rather than stopping at the first level of dependencies.

A BFS traversal will assign each cell its minimum hop distance to the target. Symbols defined within the target cell itself will be excluded from the dependency tree.

Import dependencies are straightforward: a name like `pd` requires the cell that defines it, and `pd.DataFrame` requires the `pd` binding. Function and class bodies introduce subtlety; only global names used inside them count as dependencies, while parameters and locals do not. Standard library imports still require their defining cell. Star imports, dynamic execution, and magic commands such as `%run` and `!` cannot be analyzed statically, so these cases will be documented as limitations.

Scope is limited to Python code cells. Three implementation paths were weighed: a lightweight TypeScript parser, a bundled Python script using the ast module, and leveraging Pylance’s definition provider. The TypeScript parser is fragile. Pylance matches the existing workflow but is slow and requires the language server. A bundled Python script using ast appears to be the most accurate and robust option.

Tree-sitter via WASM is too heavy. LSP-based resolution for every identifier would be too slow and flaky. The extension is TypeScript-based, yet adding a Python subprocess is acceptable because Jupyter users already have Python installed.

Vendoring a small TypeScript parser such as filbert is being considered as an alternative to a Python subprocess. The idea of reusing VS Code Jupyter's built-in concatenation and Pylance analysis was dismissed because no official Python parser library exists for this purpose. The focus is shifting toward designing the architecture.

The project's package.json and existing cell context menu and tree view implementations are being reviewed to determine whether a Python parser dependency already exists. Cell status bar items will display the dependency hop numbers, while whole-cell background highlighting is being explored for cells outside the active editor.

The VS Code API now includes `NotebookCellDecoration` and `NotebookEditor` decoration methods. Existing features like git diff highlighting and `cellMetadataDisplay` will be examined to understand cell presentation patterns. The relevant source files and package.json sections will be reviewed next.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
This is a substantial feature. The dependency analysis approach needs careful consideration.

The feature breaks down into six concrete requirements. The most critical remaining decision is how dependencies are defined, specifically whether they follow the user's existing "Go to Definition" mental model.

The dependency model is now fixed. It uses static dataflow: each cell depends on the nearest preceding cell that defines each variable it uses. A breadth-first search from the target cell assigns distances. Cells appear once at their minimum distance.

The target cell will serve as the root of the dependency tree at hop zero. It will not be numbered or highlighted as a dependency, since it is the starting point rather than a prerequisite.

The command title will be "Dependency Chain: Show Dependant Cells". It will list upstream prerequisite cells that must run first. The phrase "dependant" is kept exactly as written even though the description implies upstream dependencies.

A name defined in the same cell is not treated as an external dependency. The analysis assumes top-to-bottom execution, though notebook users frequently run cells out of order.

Pylance concatenates notebook cells into a single module. Go to Definition resolves names against this entire module, so definitions below the target cell can still be reachable. The dependency analysis should therefore treat all preceding assignments as valid prerequisites, rather than restricting itself to cells strictly above the target.

The dependency model is now fully locked. Only preceding code cells count as prerequisites. The last definition of each name wins. This matches the user's mental model of finding earlier cells that define missing variables. Imports and function definitions will also be captured as external dependencies.

Function definitions introduce a subtle dependency question. Names used inside a function body resolve at call time, not at definition time. This means a cell that defines a function does not necessarily need the cells that define its internal variables to run first. The analysis is moving toward interprocedural complexity.

The first version will approximate dependencies conservatively. Any name loaded by the cell but not defined within it counts as a prerequisite. This includes names used inside function bodies. It follows the nbdime pattern of treating all external references as upstream dependencies.

Over-approximating dependencies is safer for a minimum set. Exact runtime analysis would require a lightweight abstract interpreter to handle loops and conditionals. That complexity is too difficult for a first version.

Runtime tracing tools like ipyflow are too heavy for this feature. The implementation will instead use static analysis via Python's AST. It will leverage the existing kernel python path configuration. For each cell it will collect names assigned at the top level and names loaded from outside the cell.

The algorithm will be documented clearly with explicit limitations. It cannot handle magics, exec, star imports, or attribute access. Attribute access only creates a dependency on the root object, not on individual methods.

The parser will be implemented by spawning a Python subprocess that reads cell sources from stdin and emits per-cell definitions and uses. This leverages the existing kernel Python path and avoids adding a TypeScript tokenizer. A fallback error will appear if Python is unavailable. Python's AST is preferred over a custom tokenizer because it correctly handles strings, comments, comprehensions, and nested functions.

The analyzer will be a bundled Python script at `media/dependency_chain_analyze.py`, invoked through the kernel Python path with a fallback to the system `python` on PATH.

Cell highlighting will reuse the existing `TextEditorDecorationType` pattern. Collapsed cells and off-screen cells will remain hidden until scrolled into view.

Dependency numbers will be rendered as colored `contentText` decorations placed after the first line of each highlighted cell.

The visual design now combines two distinct signals. An orange background highlight will fade by hop distance, starting bright at distance one and becoming fainter for farther dependencies. A separate orange number glyph will sit beside each cell. Because the status bar stays visible even when a cell is collapsed, it is better suited for the numeric label than for the background highlight.

The orange background highlight will fade by hop distance using a fixed opacity scale. The dependency number will be rendered as a NotebookCellStatusBarItem with a circle-filled codicon and a numeric label. Status bar items support theme icons but not arbitrary CSS colors.

NotebookCellStatusBarItem lacks a color property, so the orange dependency number must be rendered through text decorations instead.

The visual design now pairs an orange background highlight with a bold orange number glyph on the first line of each dependency cell. A whole-cell background decoration will layer on top. An overview ruler will show these highlights in the scrollbar so off-screen cells remain visible.

The opacity scale fades by hop distance. The first hop uses an opaque orange background, while deeper hops decay by a factor of 0.72 with a minimum cap so distant dependencies stay readable.

The Dependency Chain view will likely use a flat list grouped by hop distance.

The Dependency Chain view will use a true tree structure. The target cell sits at the root. Its direct dependencies form the first level. Their direct dependencies form the second level, and so on. A cell that can be reached through multiple paths will appear only once under the closest parent. Clicking a node will jump to that cell.

Each cell will appear only once in the dependency tree. The tree nodes will display the specific symbols that create each dependency edge.

The ten-chain history will live in an in-memory ring buffer keyed by notebook URI. It will not be persisted to notebook metadata. A global or per-notebook scope is still undecided.

Per-notebook history is preferable to a global one. The last ten chains will be stored in memory and backed by workspaceState so they survive reloads within the same session. Cell indices shift when cells are inserted or deleted, so stable cell identifiers such as Jupyter nbformat cell IDs will be used instead of relying on indices.

Each saved chain snapshot will store the notebook URI, target cell identifier, per-cell hop distances, parent relationships, symbols, timestamp, and a brief label. When a user selects a chain from the history view, the extension will apply the stored hop and parent mappings directly to the current notebook. If cell indices have shifted since the snapshot was created, the view will flag the highlight as stale rather than attempting to remap.

The history view will list ten previous chains with timestamps and labels. Selecting a chain root switches the notebook highlighting to that snapshot. Clicking a cell jumps to it and makes that chain the active highlight. Stale indices will be flagged in tooltips when the first line of a cell changed.

The view will list up to ten history entries newest first. The active chain will be marked with an "(active)" label. Each entry will expand to reveal its nested dependency tree. A "Clear highlights" command will be added to the view title menu.

A context menu command will be registered for single code cells. Running a new chain will push it onto the history stack, dropping the oldest entry if the limit of ten is exceeded. The newly generated chain will become the active selection and its highlights will update automatically.

Augmented assignments like `+=` will register as both a use and a definition, with the use only if the variable was not previously defined in the cell.

The analyzer will walk the AST in execution order within each cell. A name is a use only if it has not yet been defined in that cell. Function parameters are not external dependencies. If a symbol is defined in multiple cells, the dependency edge will point to the latest preceding cell that defines it. Because edges only connect to earlier cells, the dependency graph is guaranteed to be acyclic.

BFS hop counts will label each cell. The target is hop zero. Each dependency edge adds one hop. A cell at distance d receives label d.

The tree will group cells by hop distance. Each hop level appears as a folder. The target cell sits at the root. Its direct dependencies form the first hop folder. Their dependencies form the next. This layout is clearer than a flat list.

The public npm package `@andrewhead/python-program-analysis` appears to be the original library. The private feed is only needed for some features. The key idea from `gather.ts` is a runtime dataflow analyzer that logs cell executions and slices them afterward.

Gather also supports static analysis without a kernel. It logs cells in execution order and slices them afterward. The slice returns dependent cells or lines. `smartSelect` maps that output back to notebook ranges. Pandas and numpy specs track mutations conservatively. A kernel reset clears the log. Our feature needs hop distance instead of a flat dependency set.

The public `python-program-analysis` repository should be checked for dependency graph APIs and cell-level edge types. The private feed URL can be found in the `.npmrc` file. The private feed should be avoided because it blocks CI and other contributors.

A tree with hop distances is required rather than a flat slice. The algorithm should borrow from `gatherWithoutKernel`: treat preceding cells as an execution log in notebook order, then slice backward from symbols used by the target cell. Mutation specs are essential; `df.dropna(inplace=True)` mutates state while `df = df.dropna()` creates a new definition. A simple AST without these specs would misidentify mutations and over- or under-approximate dependencies. The result must be cell-level, not line-level.

smartSelect’s mapping of slice results back to cell indices is the highlight set. Without the private package, hop distances can be built from a cell-level def-use graph. Each cell defines and uses symbols, and edges connect uses to the most recent prior definition. BFS then computes hop distances. I will check whether the public npm package exposes slice graph structure so we can reuse it.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Checking whether the slicer supports hop-level dependencies or produces flat slices.

The slicer returns a flat transitive closure rather than hop-level dependencies. The underlying def-use graph would be needed to extract hops. DataflowAnalyzer produces that graph, and the public npm package is MIT licensed.

Two paths are under consideration. The public npm package avoids the private feed but likely lacks newer specs. Alternatively, implementing cell-level def-use directly would be simpler and hop-aware, borrowing Gather's workflow of logging cells in order up to the target.

The private package adds line-level slicing and library mutation specs. These will not be replicated in v1. A dependency on the private feed is too fragile. The user wants algorithm ideas, not a dependency. The public API does not expose edges between cells directly.

Re-slicing each cell recursively would match hop distances. The target's direct dependencies are cells in its slice that do not appear in the slices of those dependencies. Immediate dependencies are those cells whose own slice excludes the target. This yields 1-jump, 2-jump, and deeper hops.

A concrete example shows why extracting hops from a transitive slicer is messy. Cell 3 depends on cells 1 and 2 transitively, but cell 2 also depends on cell 1 transitively. Isolating immediate dependencies by comparing nested slices is ambiguous. Per-cell def-use edges would allow a clean BFS traversal to layer hops.

A concrete example confirms that transitive slices alone cannot isolate immediate dependencies. The chosen approach is to build a custom cell-level def-use graph to yield clean hop distances, while adopting Gather's execution-order semantics where cells are treated as executed top-to-bottom up to the target.

Gather tracks actual execution order via `executionCount` and the execution log, unlike static source-order navigation. When no cells have been run yet, the default is to treat cells above the target as the minimum required set, matching the common "run precedents" model.

Pylance resolves Go to Definition using source order, not execution order. The v1 design deliberately follows this behavior. It will rely on document order—only cells above the target—rather than kernel execution logs. This aligns with Go to Definition and Gather’s `gatherWithoutKernel` approach.

Execution-log mode can be added later as a future enhancement.

Cell-level highlighting is the right granularity for whole-cell selection. Recording which specific names cause each dependency edge improves UX over Gather’s range-based smart select.

Naive AST analysis misses mutating APIs such as `inplace=True`. Gather’s specs handle these cases. v1 should document this limitation.

A lightweight workaround replaces the private spec feed. A small built-in rule treats calls with `inplace=True` or known mutators as redefining the receiver object. The next use then depends on this cell rather than the original constructor. This captures the highest-value spec insight without the private package.

Gather flags edited cells as stale. The v1 design will cache dependency chains as snapshots. It will not recompute them automatically when cells change. Users must request a fresh chain.

Mapping slice text back to cells via `includes` is fragile. The history will instead store cell indices and Jupyter cell IDs directly. This prevents re-matching text during selection.

Gather uses `cell.document.uri.fragment` as a persistent cell ID. The v1 design should adopt the same pattern so history can remap if cell indices shift.

The public npm package is outdated and line-slicer oriented. It does not expose hop edges cleanly. A custom cell-level def-use graph is a better fit for numbered hops.

Gather may fail on IPython magics. The parser should strip `%` and `!` lines before analyzing cells.

The concrete algorithm compares each cell against all preceding cells to build a directed dependency graph. Each edge is labeled with the variable name that creates the link. A BFS traversal from the target cell assigns a minimum hop distance to every cell, and the tree parent is simply the BFS predecessor.

Unresolved names will be listed on the target node.

The visual design follows git diff decoration. Orange alpha fades by hop depth, and a hop count appears before the cell content text.

The view will show ten history roots as a nested tree. Clicking a cell reveals its details, and clicking a history entry switches the active highlight.

The dependency chain will live under `src/dependencyChain/`. The command title will spell the word as "Dependant" to match the user's request. The symbol analyzer can be pure TypeScript or can spawn Python.

A Python subprocess using the standard library `ast` module is the chosen approach. It avoids the private npm feed and provides more accurate parsing than a hand-rolled TypeScript walker. The repository already spawns child processes for git, so this fits the existing pattern.

The Python AST script will be bundled inside the extension. It will be invoked through the kernel Python path setting, falling back to the system `python` on PATH. The script returns per-cell definitions, uses, and mutated names. Graph construction and hop computation remain in TypeScript and are unit-tested without Python. If the script fails, the view will display an error with the unresolved reason.

The Python AST script will strip IPython magics before parsing. On SyntaxError, it returns empty symbol sets and a parseError flag so the tree can report that cell could not be parsed.

The script will walk the AST sequentially with a scope stack. Assignments add names to `defines` only after the right-hand side is fully traversed. Loads of names not yet defined locally in that cell are recorded as `uses`. Imports bind names to `defines`.

Function and class definitions bind names at the cell level. Their bodies are walked with a fresh scope. Loads of names outside the function are treated as cell-level uses. This over-approximation risks pulling in extra cells. Gather avoids this by including only the function body lines that actually affect the seed statement.

A compromise for function-free-variable resolution avoids both over-inclusion and under-inclusion. Loads of names defined in the cell are treated as uses. Free variables of a function are only included if that function is called within the cell. This yields a tighter minimum set than a naive body walk, because undefined functions will not trigger NameErrors.

The symbol analyzer will walk the call graph within each cell. It will include free variables of functions that are directly invoked, and recursively include free variables of any nested functions called by those functions. This limits the scope to one level of direct calls rather than full interprocedural analysis.

Free variables of function bodies must be treated as uses of the defining cell. A caller cell only records the function name as a use, not the underlying free variables. Because the caller does not execute the function body, it cannot resolve those variables itself. The dependency therefore belongs to the defining cell, which must be run to satisfy the call.

The dependency model is conservative and correct for ensuring a cell succeeds when its dependents are run. Even if a function is never called by the target chain, its defining cell is still included because Gather erringly includes uncertain dependencies. This is stated explicitly.

Mutating API calls and assignments will be tracked as state updates. Calls with `inplace=True` or known mutating methods such as `list.append` and `dict.update` will mark the receiver as both defined and used. Subscript assignments like `obj.loc[...] =` and `AugAssign` nodes such as `x += 1` will also be recorded as mutations. The next cell that references the same name will depend on this cell.

History will be kept in memory per notebook URI, capped at ten entries, newest first. Selecting a history entry will not trigger a recomputation. Each snapshot stores the hop map, tree, symbol labels, timestamp, target index, and target first line.

When switching between history entries, the view will clear the previous decorations and apply only the newly selected chain. The target cell will appear as the tree root without orange numbering or special highlighting.

The command will be restricted to Python code cells. If the active cell has a non-Python language ID, the handler will display a message stating that only Python is supported.

The command will be available whenever a notebook is active. A clear button will sit in the view title. Decorations will be reapplied to visible text editors, following the GitDiffCellHighlighter pattern. Line zero will carry a number decoration with color, background, and margin, plus a whole-cell background. Opacity will fade with hop depth, and the overview ruler will share the same color. The plan is ready to create.

The user’s note about the private feed signals that the extension must not depend on that package. Cell-level granularity is already confirmed, so no further questions are needed. I will now create the plan.

_**Agent (default)**_

Right-click a Python code cell and choose **Dependency Chain: Show Dependant Cells**. The extension finds the earlier cells that must run first, paints them in orange by hop distance, and lists the chain in a new **Dependency Chain** view.

- **1** is the brightest orange and marks cells that directly define a name this cell uses. **2**, **3**, and so on are the same orange, faded, for cells those depend on. Each cell is numbered once, at its shortest hop. The cell you clicked is the root of the tree and is not painted.
- The view keeps the last 10 chains for the open notebook. Click a chain to restore its highlighting without analyzing again. Click a cell in the tree to jump to it. **Dependency Chain: Clear Highlights** removes the paint.
- Names with no earlier cell, `import *`, and cells that fail to parse are called out on the tree instead of being guessed. Analysis uses Python's `ast` module, so `python` must be on `PATH`, or `jupyter-cell-tags.jupyterEnhancements.kernel.pythonPath` must point at an existing interpreter.
